routes.description: Establish a historically credible body of postmortem-appearance data, defend supernatural events as admissible historical conclusions, and show that resurrection explains the relevant data better than the principal naturalistic alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the appearance traditions are sufficiently established, resurrection has greater comparative explanatory adequacy than rival accounts, and neither methodological naturalism nor uncertainty about the precise divine agent blocks the supernatural conclusion.

motionBridge.description: The historical evidence and relevant background information must make Jesus's resurrection the best explanation of the reported postmortem appearances.

centralBridges.description: Early and corroborated sources must establish individual, hostile, and group appearance claims as data requiring explanation.
Resurrection must provide greater explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and economy than hallucination or other naturalistic alternatives.
Historical inquiry must be able to recognize an event transcending known natural capacities without first identifying its precise supernatural agent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Independent allegedly paranormal phenomena may supply background plausibility for admitting supernatural explanations.
Reliable ordinary testimonial evidence must be capable in principle of supporting an extraordinary historical event.

routes.description: Maintain that resurrection proponents bear the evidential burden, challenge the accessibility and reliability of the ancient appearance reports, and deny that unexplained events or defeated natural alternatives establish supernatural causation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical data remain insufficiently confirmed or if resurrection and divine agency cannot be warranted from those data, making suspension of belief appropriate without requiring proof that resurrection was impossible.

motionBridge.description: Belief in Jesus's resurrection must be withheld unless the affirmative evidence establishes both the alleged event and the inferential move to resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Ancient appearance reports must provide accessible, independently supportable evidence adequate to establish the claimed postmortem events.
An unexplained or anomalous event must not be treated as evidence of supernatural causation without a method that distinguishes that cause from error, fraud, hallucination, or unknown natural causes.
The resurrection hypothesis must supply testable or discriminating explanatory content rather than merely relabeling the absence of a natural explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The evidential limits created by two millennia of investigative distance must constrain comparisons with directly observable modern anomalies.
Attributing resurrection to divine action requires independent grounds for a capable and willing agent or evidence that itself discriminates in favor of such an agent.

sections.title: Historical foundation for the appearance claims
sections.rationale: The existence, independence, accessibility, and reliability of the Pauline, apostolic, individual, and group appearance traditions determine what historical data the competing explanations must address.

sections.title: Resurrection versus naturalistic explanations
sections.rationale: The motion turns centrally on whether resurrection explains the asserted historical data better than hallucination, error, dishonesty, or other naturalistic possibilities under comparative explanatory criteria.

sections.title: From anomaly to supernatural causation
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether an event judged incompatible with known natural capacities may be classified as supernatural or whether that classification merely substitutes a label for unresolved causation.

sections.title: Historical method and standards for extraordinary claims
sections.rationale: The parties' competing standards for testimony, repeatability, methodological naturalism, and investigation determine what kinds of evidence can justify an extraordinary historical conclusion.

sections.title: Background supernaturalism and identification of divine agency
sections.rationale: Allegedly paranormal phenomena and the question of prior grounds for God affect the background plausibility of resurrection and the further inference from a postmortem event to purposeful divine action.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Multiple classes of allegedly paranormal experience collectively provide empirical support for a supernatural dimension of reality.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Licona immediately before this uninterrupted opening-statement segment, and the speaker explicitly identifies his first major contention.

response.rationale: This constructive move introduces cumulative paranormal reports as background support for admitting a supernatural dimension; it does not answer an earlier opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states a supporting contention and announces multiple evidential lines, though the rendered evidence does not display their full defense.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative proposition is recoverable, but the operative meaning of supernatural dimension and the evidential status of the reported classes remain only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that empirical data strongly suggest a supernatural dimension outruns the excerpted announcement, which supplies no visible verification or rival comparison.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A cumulative-evidence inference is coherent, but the bridge from several anomalous experience classes to a supernatural dimension remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The source announces four evidential lines but the selected evidence does not show representative verification, independence analysis, or comparison with ordinary explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the subsidiary background-supernaturalism bridge and sits near the top of that tier because this is its express purpose.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move principally advances its own cumulative background case and does not meaningfully interpret a developed opposing alternative in this span.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona expressly says empirical data strongly suggest a supernatural dimension and announces four lines of evidence, beginning with paranormal experiences.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Early Pauline material and apostolic corroboration support a historical bedrock of individual, hostile, and group resurrection-appearance experiences.
moves.attributionBasis: This remains within Licona's uninterrupted opening statement, and the speaker expressly transitions to his second major contention concerning historical data.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the affirmative historical data set through Paul, his apostolic contacts, and asserted individual and group appearance experiences.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly establishes an indispensable historical premise and identifies both its source route and the appearance data claimed as bedrock.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-based proposition is clear, though the scope of scholarly agreement and the distinction between belief, experience, and veridical appearance are compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Paul's early status and apostolic contact warrant historical significance, but the broad virtually-undisputed framing and full bedrock conclusion need qualification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from an early claimed eyewitness acquainted with disciples to early shared appearance belief is coherent, with one bounded bridge concerning corroboration and independence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul's claimed eyewitness status and contact with disciples are specific support, but independence, textual details, and the move from reports to group experiences remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This move expressly supplies the early and corroborated appearance material required by the central historical-bedrock bridge and is maximally relevant within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents affirmative source evidence without directly construing or evaluating a developed skeptical alternative in the selected span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies Paul as an early claimed eyewitness who knew Jesus's disciples and preached their message, then states individual and group appearance experiences.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Under explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and avoidance of ad hoc assumptions, resurrection explains the asserted historical bedrock better than hallucination.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted Licona opening continues through a methodological comparison and ends with his stated conclusion followed by audience applause.

response.rationale: This constructive move applies explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and ad hocness to compare resurrection with the hallucination hypothesis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies comparative criteria and applies them to a principal rival, although the complete comparison and supporting literature are compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition and criteria are recoverable and stable, with an implicit qualification that the result depends on accepting the asserted historical facts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Comparative probability is the right force, but the brief treatment of Paul and group hallucination leaves the superiority conclusion somewhat stronger than the displayed warrant.

charity.alternative: Hallucination can explain the appearance reports without invoking resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: It must also account for hostile and group experiences under the accepted bedrock.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The criteria-based comparison is valid in form and identifies expected-data differences, while the assumptions about grief and group hallucinations leave bounded implicit bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific considerations involving Paul and groups are offered, but their psychological and historical warrants and serious alternative variants are not defended in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly performs the comparative explanation required by a central bridge and is at the top of its relevance tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move grants hallucination explanatory scope and low ad hocness before criticizing power and plausibility, though the rival's strongest variants are not developed.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona grants hallucination explanatory scope and limited ad hocness but argues it lacks power and plausibility for Paul and alleged group appearances.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Belief in resurrection should be withheld unless its proponents discharge their evidential burden and show that the skeptical default is false.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives the floor to Matt Dillahunty, who identifies his position as being unconvinced and develops the null-hypothesis framework.

components.text: Whether the affirmative comparison actually establishes resurrection as superior to the skeptical default.
Whether the asserted historical bedrock is evidentially sufficient to warrant belief.

response.rationale: The move contacts the decisive burden underlying the affirmative historical and comparative case by requiring the proponent to displace evidential withholding, though it does not yet rebut each item.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer: it contacts the decisive burden and default but does not examine the particular historical sources or comparative criteria already offered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The withholding rule is clear, although the analogy between statistical null hypotheses and ordinary historical belief carries an implicit domain qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Assigning proponents a burden is warranted, but describing the null as assumed true rather than a position of withholding slightly overstates the default.

charity.alternative: The affirmative need only show resurrection is comparatively best, not prove skepticism false with certainty.
charity.decisiveQualification: Comparative superiority still requires sufficient evidence to overcome withholding.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The burden allocation coherently supports withholding, but the description of an unconfirmable null being assumed true introduces a material ambiguity between disbelief and nonbelief.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument rests mostly on a general evidential norm and a legal analogy; these support burden allocation but do not themselves assess the resurrection evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly states the motion-level condition for withholding belief and therefore has near-maximal relevance within the motion tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly places the burden on the affirmative, but its null-hypothesis language risks making the opposing burden sound more absolute than necessary.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty invokes a null-hypothesis default and says the proponent must demonstrate that its proposal is superior by showing the default false.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Reports of unexplained experiences do not establish a supernatural realm when that category remains poorly defined, unconfirmed, and causally uninvestigated.
moves.attributionBasis: This is an uninterrupted part of Dillahunty's opening, marked by first-person references to his magician background and his skeptical methodological position.

components.text: Whether classes of unexplained experience collectively warrant a supernatural dimension.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the inference's defect: supernatural is poorly defined and unconfirmed, so reports attributed to it cannot establish that causal category without investigation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the decisive inference from anomalous reports to supernatural reality and states the defeating consequence, qualifying as a strong diagnostic defeat.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition clearly distinguishes reports attributed to the supernatural from confirmation that a supernatural realm or cause exists.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move does not claim anomalies are false; it makes the appropriately limited claim that unexplained reports do not establish the proposed category.

charity.alternative: Several independent anomaly classes may cumulatively support supernaturalism without individually proving it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cumulative force still depends on defined terms, reliable cases, and exclusion of ordinary causes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between unexplained experience and established supernatural ontology is explicit and directly defeats the unsupported causal inference, with only minor definitional compression.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is principally methodological and well matched to the limited conclusion, though no representative paranormal case is examined in the selected evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the subsidiary background-supernaturalism bridge and is highly relevant within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The criticism preserves the possibility of testing attributed claims and targets confirmation rather than dismissing every reported anomaly as fabricated.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty says supernatural is poorly defined and has not been confirmed, while allowing investigation of claims merely attributed to supernatural causes.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Eliminating a hoax or lacking a natural explanation does not establish resurrection, because attributing the event to divine action supplies no mechanism or explanatory content.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty remains the uninterrupted speaker and explicitly applies his earlier methodological criticism to resurrection arguments and an apologetic dichotomy.

components.text: Whether resurrection has explanatory power sufficient to outperform naturalistic hypotheses.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses that eliminating alternatives or invoking God does not add causal content, and concludes that the proposed explanation has not solved the explanatory problem.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly attacks the decisive explanatory-power inference and states why the resurrection label fails to provide the content required by the affirmative comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between ruling out a rival and providing a positive causal explanation is clear, stable, and explicitly applied to resurrection.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Requiring positive explanatory content is apt, but saying supernatural explanation has no content at all is somewhat broader than the displayed argument establishes.

charity.alternative: Divine resurrection can explain the appearances even without describing a physical mechanism.
charity.decisiveQualification: It must still add discriminating content beyond the absence of an accepted natural explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The non-elimination and positive-content critique is logically strong, though the further equation of divine action with a contentless mystery is somewhat compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument relies on an explicit explanatory norm and applies it directly; it does not, however, examine all content the affirmative hypothesis might include.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central comparative-explanation bridge at its decisive requirement of explanatory power.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately presses the need for positive content, though equating every divine explanation with magic understates possible agent-intention explanations.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty asks how divine resurrection became most plausible and argues that appeal to a larger mystery supplies no mechanism or explanatory content.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Treating resurrection as plausible presupposes independent grounds for a God capable of and willing to raise Jesus, while private revelation is unverifiable hearsay to outsiders.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted skeptical opening continues, with the speaker contrasting theological and philosophical approaches before identifying their required divine premise.

components.text: Whether resurrection is plausible without antecedent grounds for a capable and willing agent.
Whether generic supernatural background evidence supports the specific divine-agent inference.

response.rationale: The move directly raises a missing prior premise for the affirmative hypothesis and distinguishes generic supernaturalism from evidence for a resurrection-capable God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully contacts the agent-plausibility component, although it does not answer every historical or comparative element of the affirmative case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The required-agent premise is clear, but the claim that one must already believe it to assess plausibility blurs prior probability with absolute prerequisite.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Independent grounds would strengthen the hypothesis, but calling prior belief a necessary component excludes the possibility that event evidence updates agent probability.

charity.alternative: Resurrection evidence may itself provide grounds for belief in a capable divine agent.
charity.decisiveQualification: The evidence must discriminate that agent from other unknown causes rather than presuppose it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The background-probability point is coherent, but the necessity claim contains a material unsupported bridge from needing agent content to needing prior belief.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited debate precedent illustrates the premise but does not establish its necessity, and the private-revelation concern is asserted rather than developed here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly supports the subsidiary theistic-background bridge and sits at the top of that relevance tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies a real background-plausibility issue but overstates it as a strict prerequisite and underplays evidential updating from the event itself.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty says a resurrection argument requires a God capable of and desirous of resurrection and treats that premise as necessary for plausibility.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Neither historical inquiry nor science can confirm supernatural causation without a workable account of what the supernatural is and how it causally operates.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty remains the sole speaker and explicitly turns from the limits of direct scientific investigation to the historical method used by Licona.

components.text: Whether historical comparison can establish a supernatural resurrection cause.
Whether attributed supernatural claims can confirm a supernatural causal category.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the missing causal-discrimination method and concludes that neither scientific nor historical inquiry can confirm the asserted supernatural connection without it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly diagnoses a central inferential gap, though the categorical statement about every possible historical method is broader than the argument supplied.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal-method demand is clear, but the scope shifts from present inability to investigate a cause to a broad limitation on historical and scientific confirmation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A discriminating causal method is reasonably required, while saying inquiry is barred until supernatural ontology is understood imposes a somewhat stronger condition than defended.

charity.alternative: Historical inference may identify extraordinary causation from effects without a complete causal mechanism.
charity.decisiveQualification: The effects must discriminate supernatural causation from unknown natural causes and error.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from absent causal discrimination to withheld causal attribution is strong, with a bounded overreach concerning what all historical inquiry can confirm.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological distinction between investigating claims and establishing causes supports the conclusion, though no detailed competing causal protocol is assessed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central supernatural-admissibility bridge and its required historical causal inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move properly demands discrimination but gives limited consideration to ordinary abductive inference from effects despite incomplete mechanisms.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty distinguishes investigating claims attributed to the supernatural from developing a causal connection and demands an account of what the supernatural is.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Scientific and historical disciplines use different investigative methods, so lack of controlled repeatability does not by itself disqualify supernatural claims from investigation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Licona, who explicitly frames the passage as his rebuttal to Dillahunty's opening objections.

components.text: Whether absence of controlled scientific repeatability bars investigation of supernatural claims.
Whether paranormal evidence may be investigated under methods appropriate to its discipline.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the alleged methodological bar by distinguishing discipline-specific methods, but it does not supply the causal-discrimination procedure the con move principally demanded.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer: it rebuts a repeatability requirement but leaves the deeper demand for distinguishing supernatural causation from alternatives unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The discipline-specific-method proposition is clear, with an implicit qualification that methodological diversity does not eliminate standards of causal discrimination.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that lack of laboratory repeatability does not itself disqualify investigation fits the methodological observation, subject to an implicit evidential qualification.

charity.alternative: The skeptical demand concerns causal confirmation, not one universal laboratory method.
charity.decisiveQualification: Discipline-specific inquiry still needs reliable tests that distinguish rival causes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from methodological pluralism to investigability is coherent, though it does not establish that historical methods can identify a supernatural cause.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The general fact of discipline-specific methods supports the narrow conclusion, but no concrete historical validation procedure is supplied for the disputed claims.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move attacks the subsidiary investigative-distance and methodology concern, with high relevance inside that tier but incomplete causal contact.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly rejects a single-method requirement but materially narrows the skeptical challenge by treating it mainly as a demand for scientific testing.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona lists paranormal phenomena, near-death experiences, apparitions, and answered prayer, then argues that scientific disciplines employ different methods rather than one universal test.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Methodological naturalism can exclude supernatural explanations in advance and prevent recognition of events that known natural causes cannot plausibly explain.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona continues his rebuttal in a sustained first-person critique, with no speaker transition before the next topic.

components.text: Whether methodological naturalism improperly excludes supernatural explanations before comparison.
Whether an extraordinary information-bearing event can count against ordinary causal explanations.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the exclusion concern with a concrete anomalous-information hypothetical, but it does not fully answer how the supernatural cause is distinguished from every unknown alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer because it exposes possible prior exclusion while leaving the opponent's demand for a workable positive causal method only partly answered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anti-exclusion proposition is clear and stable, subject to the implicit condition that known natural explanations have genuinely been tested and found implausible.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hypothetical shows that automatic exclusion can distort comparison, but it does not establish that the actual resurrection evidence meets the hypothetical's evidential strength.

charity.alternative: Methodological naturalism withholds supernatural attribution without denying anomalous events.
charity.decisiveQualification: Withholding is legitimate unless evidence discriminates supernatural from unknown natural causes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The hypothetical coherently challenges a rule of automatic exclusion, though moving from an unexplained private-information event to miracle remains a bounded inferential gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The illustrative hypothetical has intuitive force but is not actual case evidence and does not demonstrate that resurrection or paranormal reports satisfy its conditions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the con central causal-underdetermination bridge by challenging categorical methodological exclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies the danger of prior exclusion but partly treats methodological restraint as if it necessarily ranked every natural explanation above any supernatural one.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona offers a hypothetical involving inaccessible private information and argues that always preferring hallucination would embody methodological naturalism rather than neutral comparison.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Case-by-case comparison of hypotheses using the historical data and relevant background information favors resurrection over the proposed naturalistic alternatives.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains Licona's uninterrupted rebuttal and repeatedly restates his historical-hypothesis methodology in the first person.

components.text: Whether controlled historical comparison can discharge the affirmative burden.
Whether resurrection can be compared as a substantive historical hypothesis.
Whether historical method can assess a supernatural conclusion case by case.

response.rationale: The reply directly proposes historical hypothesis comparison as the means of meeting the burden and asserts a result across naturalistic rivals, while compressing the actual comparisons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts all three methodological demands, but the assertion that resurrection wins every comparison lacks the displayed analysis needed for a fully explicit answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative method and conclusion are clear, with an implicit dependence on the accuracy and completeness of the known historical data and rival set.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying resurrection comes out on top every time is categorical, while the excerpt admits only hallucination was shown and supplies no analysis of all other rivals.

charity.alternative: Naturalistic hypotheses or suspension may remain preferable because the data and causal method are underdetermined.
charity.decisiveQualification: Each rival and the resurrection hypothesis require symmetrical comparison using established data.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative procedure is coherent, but the move from one sketched hallucination comparison to victory over every naturalistic hypothesis is a material unsupported generalization.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The decisive universal result is largely asserted; the selected evidence supplies neither the rival-by-rival analysis nor verification of the assumed historical data.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly claims to satisfy the motion-level comparative burden through controlled historical hypothesis assessment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move endorses case-by-case comparison but does not present the strongest versions of the other naturalistic hypotheses before declaring universal superiority.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona describes formulating hypotheses from known data and weighing them for probability, then says resurrection defeats all naturalistic hypotheses although only hallucination was presented.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Methodological naturalism permits investigation of extraordinary events but withholds supernatural attribution until a testable model distinguishes genuine phenomena from fraud, error, and hallucination.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator announces Dillahunty's rebuttal, after which he directly answers Licona's claims in a continuous monologue.

components.text: Whether methodological naturalism excludes investigation or only withholds supernatural attribution.
Whether discipline-specific methods presently confirm a supernatural causal category.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes testing extraordinary claims from attributing them to the supernatural, thereby diagnosing the pro move's conflation and preserving investigation while withholding causal judgment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly answers the methodological-exclusion charge and states the consequence: anomalous events remain investigable, but attribution awaits confirmable discrimination.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between investigating an event and confirming a supernatural attribution is explicit, consistent, and carefully scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The requirement to test before causal attribution fits the limited skeptical conclusion and does not deny that extraordinary events may occur or be investigated.

charity.alternative: Methodological naturalism may function as an a priori ban on supernatural explanations.
charity.decisiveQualification: A test-first policy need not ban investigation or permanently exclude a supported supernatural model.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The event-investigation versus causal-attribution distinction is explicit, consistent, and resolves the strongest charge that methodological naturalism simply bars inquiry.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological warrant is clearly defended with the comet example, though a fully specified threshold for confirming a supernatural model remains absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central causal-underdetermination bridge by specifying the required order of investigation and attribution.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply squarely distinguishes prior exclusion from provisional withholding and expressly allows scientists to investigate even striking extraordinary events.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty says methodological naturalism does not bar testing attributed claims, including an extraordinary comet event, but withholds supernatural appeal pending confirmation.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Paul is a weak foundation for resurrection because he lacked direct access to Jesus's ministry, death, burial, and empty tomb, while surviving reports do not independently demonstrate a return from death.
moves.attributionBasis: The first-person skeptical assessment remains part of Dillahunty's announced rebuttal and ends immediately before the moderator changes formats.

components.text: Whether Paul and surviving reports adequately establish the asserted appearance bedrock.
Whether the known data are sufficiently secure for comparative historical inference.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges Paul's access to the underlying ministry, death, burial, and tomb events, but only partly addresses his claimed appearance and apostolic corroboration.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the decisive source-sufficiency issue but leaves Paul's own claimed experience and contact with disciples substantially unexamined.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-access criticism is clear and explicitly limited to what Paul did not directly witness during Jesus's life, death, burial, and tomb history.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The access limitations weaken several historical claims, but they do not alone establish that Paul is weak evidence for his own experience or inherited traditions.

charity.alternative: Paul is valuable because he is early, claims an appearance, and knew leading disciples.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those advantages do not give him direct access to every event underlying the resurrection narrative.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from lack of direct access to reduced warrant for specific events is sound, while the broader conclusion about resurrection evidence needs additional source analysis.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names concrete limitations concerning ministry, crucifixion, burial, and tomb access, but does not assess Paul's letters, traditions, or apostolic meetings in detail.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly attacks the central historical-bedrock bridge by contesting the affirmative's principal early source.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explicitly grants scholarly regard for Paul as the best source before isolating his access limitations, though it underdevelops his positive evidential features.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty grants Paul's status as a leading source but notes that he never met the living Jesus and did not witness the death, burial, or empty tomb.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Calling an event supernatural merely labels the absence of a natural explanation and cannot justify specific conclusions about gods, spirits, souls, or resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Within the alternating questioning, Dillahunty explicitly identifies the repeated explanatory pattern and develops a continuous skeptical challenge.

components.text: Whether inability to account naturally for an event identifies a supernatural cause.
Whether failed natural explanations positively establish resurrection.

response.rationale: The move contacts the decisive inference by emphasizing that lack of a current natural account does not identify the proposed cause, though the excerpt's interrupted exchange limits elaboration.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly reaches the causal-label problem and the repeated cannot-account-for inference, but provides less explicit development than the earlier methodological critique.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition consistently distinguishes absence of a present natural account from positive identification of a supernatural or resurrection cause.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that explanatory failure does not itself identify a cause is appropriately forceful and expressly tied to what is presently known.

charity.alternative: An event impossible under known laws may reasonably be called supernatural without naming its agent.
charity.decisiveQualification: Known-law incompatibility must be established and still does not identify resurrection or a particular agent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The underdetermination inference is straightforward and valid: inability to account for an event naturally does not entail a particular supernatural cause.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is a strong general causal principle, though the selected exchange does not supply a detailed application to every resurrection datum.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central causal-underdetermination bridge at its decisive inferential point.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately preserves the distinction between anomaly and specific causal verdict, although the brief exchange does not fully develop the opponent's definitional position.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty identifies the repeated move from inability to account for something under present knowledge to a stronger supernatural causal conclusion.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The claim that Jesus appeared to five hundred people lacks accessible identities, statements, and experiences sufficient to investigate whether the reported event occurred.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Dillahunty's comment, and his first-person response continues until the moderator resumes speaking.

components.text: Whether the reported group appearance to five hundred supplies investigable historical data.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the accessibility of the five-hundred claim by pointing to absent identities and experiences, while leaving other individual and group traditions untouched.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer because it contacts a decisive group-evidence component but does not answer the full Pauline and apostolic bedrock.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criticism is clearly and narrowly scoped to the historical investigability and evidential sufficiency of the reported five-hundred appearance.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker appropriately states personal evidential insufficiency rather than certainty that the report was false, matching the limited accessibility critique.

charity.alternative: An early report that many witnesses remained alive could function as a checkable public claim.
charity.decisiveQualification: Modern evaluation lacks their identities, statements, and independent experiential records.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from inaccessible witness identities and experiences to limited present investigability is explicit and contains no major logical gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The criticism identifies concrete missing evidence—witness identities, experiences, and investigatory access—while avoiding the stronger unsupported claim that the event never occurred.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks a material component of the central historical-bedrock bridge, though not the entire source complex.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not deny that more information might exist or that the report could be true; it targets the evidence presently available for investigation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty says the five-hundred report cannot presently be investigated and insists occurrence must be established before debating a group-hallucination explanation.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: An extraordinary event does not require a special category of extraordinary evidence when sufficiently good ordinary eyewitness evidence supports it.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator offers Licona a reply, and Licona develops his beheading hypothetical until Dillahunty answers his distinction between event and evidence.

components.text: Whether extraordinary-event evidence must be extraordinary in kind rather than sufficiently good testimony.
What quality of evidence may in principle discharge the affirmative burden.

response.rationale: The reply directly disputes a special-category evidence requirement through an eyewitness hypothetical, but it does not show that the ancient testimony is comparably good or accessible.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer reaches the general standard but leaves the opponent's case-specific demand for accessible evidence about the five hundred unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ordinary-good-testimony proposition is recoverable, but extraordinary evidence shifts between evidential quality, evidential type, and direct observation in the exchange.
